name: leerob.com
object_type: Portfolio, but only in the loosest sense — it is a personal writing site that happens to serve the function a portfolio usually serves. There is no project gallery, no skills list, no resume, and no work-sample grid; /resume and /uses both 308-redirect to the homepage, i.e. they were deliberately removed. What replaces them is a 28-essay corpus at one-word URLs plus two narrative career pages (/cursor, /vercel) and a narrative life story (/bio). Closer to a publication or an author page than to a job-application artifact, and it is the clearest counter-model in this research set: proof by body-of-work rather than proof by card grid.
format_genre: Writing-led, and about as pure an example as exists. The homepage is a single `<main>` containing an `<h1>`, four short paragraphs and a six-item link list — no hero image, no header nav, no footer, no social row, no cards, no sections. Every route is the same template: title, a grey byline/date line, prose. The typographic system is a reading system: STIX Two Text (a serif designed for scientific publishing) as the document font, a ~60–65ch measure, generous leading. Individual essays escalate into rich long-form documents — /ai is a ~180 KB page carrying seven bespoke interactive visualisations (tokenization, embeddings, self-attention, next-token prediction, temperature, training loop, RLHF) and 14 footnotes — but the frame never stops being an article.
intent_audience: Personal brand / authority-building, with a quiet deal-flow funnel underneath. It is emphatically NOT job-seeking: no resume, no availability line, no 'hire me', no skills matrix, nothing an ATS could parse. The conversion the site actually optimises for is stated in one sentence at the very end of the homepage: 'I also make videos, advise companies, and do angel investing. Reach out if interested.' That is the entire CTA — one mailto, no form, no Calendly, no rate card, no portfolio-of-investments page. Audience is peers, founders and hiring-side operators who already know the name; the site's job is to convert reputation into inbound advising/angel conversations and to keep the teaching brand ('My life's work is to make technology easy to understand and interesting to learn about') compounding. Secondary audience: developers learning AI — /ai plus a 45-term glossary corpus function as a free educational product.
seniority_stage: Senior/staff-plus and effectively post-career-search — the endpoint of the trajectory the rest of this research set is climbing. Fifteen years coding, five years at Vercel taken from IC to VP of Developer Experience, then a lateral move to Cursor (joined at ~70 employees, July 2025) where he first worked as a cross-functional generalist and, as of June 2026, moved onto the ML team to work on model behaviour and personality. He also advises companies and angel-invests. 'Good' for this item means authority, distribution and readability, not legibility to a recruiter — and the site is engineered for exactly that. The important corollary for the report: almost nothing about this site's *structure* is transferable to a junior or mid-level engineer, because the structure presupposes an audience that already arrived knowing who he is. What IS transferable is its craft discipline: the URL scheme, the byline pattern, the archived links, the narrative career pages.
language_i18n: English only. `<html lang="en">`, all copy in English, no language switcher, no localised routes, no hreflang. There is no EN/RU toggle or any i18n machinery at all — the site's reach strategy is distribution (X, YouTube, newsletter) rather than translation.
owner_role: Lee Robinson — opens with 'I'm an engineer and writer.' Current: works on ML at Cursor, 'helping improve model behavior and personality' (moved to ML in June 2026; joined Cursor July 2025 at ~70 employees, initially a generalist across engineering, product and marketing, created and maintained Cursor's docs and learning courses, spoke on context engineering and the Composer model, played pseudo-PM on launches). Previously five years at Vercel, joining in 2020 when it was 30 people at ~$1M ARR and leaving in July 2025 when it was 650 people at $200M+ ARR, going from IC to VP of Developer Experience across DevRel, product, community and docs. Iowa State University, computer engineering. Based in Des Moines, Iowa; works remotely. Also: YouTube creator, angel investor, company advisor. Personal framing is unusually forward: 'I'm a husband, father, and a massive music fan.' Note a stale artifact — the JSON-LD Person block still declares `jobTitle: "VP of Developer Experience"` while `worksFor` is Cursor, contradicting the body copy.
sections_present: Present, but none of them look like a portfolio section. About → /bio, a long-form narrative titled 'My life in five minutes' (childhood, October Sky, model rockets, Iowa, forums, pirated Sony Vegas, building a PC at 14, Iowa State, internships, Vercel, fatherhood, Cursor) with embedded video clips and expandable spoiler blocks. Experience → two dated narrative pages, /cursor ('July 2025 – Present') and /vercel ('5 Things I Learned From 5 Years At Vercel', July 2025), i.e. employment history written as essays rather than bullet lists. Blog → /writing, a flat chronological list of 28 essays. Contact → a single inline mailto in the last sentence of the homepage. Skills → the closest thing is /stack ('My Stack': Next.js/React/TypeScript, Tailwind + shadcn/ui, Postgres + Drizzle, Cursor, coding patterns/AGENTS.md), written as an opinionated essay rather than a competency list. Extra sections with no portfolio analogue: /beliefs ('Things I Believe'), /bookmarks (a large curated links library organised into Tools / Articles / Productivity / Craft / Engineering, plus guitar tabs), /music (Spotify top artists and tracks), and a 45-entry AI glossary corpus. ABSENT: Projects/Portfolio (no gallery, no cards, no demos), Resume/CV (/resume 308→/), Uses (/uses 308→/), Skills list, Testimonials, Services, Now page, Newsletter signup, Speaking page, Investments page.
nav_pattern: Multi-page, and radically chrome-free — arguably the most aggressive navigation minimalism in this research set. There is **no header, no nav bar, no footer, and no social-links row on any page**; the served HTML for every route is literally `<main>` containing an `<h1>`, a byline, and prose. The only persistent navigational affordance is the byline itself: the grey line under each title ('By Lee Robinson', 'November 2024 (updated 2026) – Lee Robinson', 'July 2025 – Present') is an `<a href="/">` — the author credit doubles as the home link. Everything else is in-prose links. Routing is the design: every page lives at a one-word top-level slug (/ai, /agents, /css, /stack, /bio, /beliefs, /music, /rust, /docs, /devrel, /dx, /heroku, /compression, /pixo, /bronco, /bookmarks…), which makes URLs memorable, quotable in a talk, and typeable from memory. A Postgres-backed redirects table (per the template repo) keeps old paths alive. Discovery has an obvious cost: nothing is browsable without either the homepage's six hand-picked links or /writing, and there is no search, no tag index, and no RSS.
visual_style: Editorial minimalism, executed with unusual restraint. Effectively no decoration: no hero, no illustration, no avatar on the page (an avatar.png exists but is only referenced in JSON-LD), no borders, no cards, no shadows, no gradients, no icons in the chrome. Content is a single centred column with a 60–65ch measure, top-margin-only on desktop (`mt-0 md:mt-16`). Design-trend alignment: it consciously sits outside the trend cycle — not bento grid, not neo-brutalism, not glassmorphism, not kinetic typography. If it aligns with anything current it is the 2024–2026 'personal-site-as-serif-blog' countertrend (the Bear Blog / Gwern / rauno / plaintext lineage), where the visual signal is 'I have nothing to prove with chrome'. The visual richness is pushed entirely into the content layer instead: essays contain bordered, rounded, dark-mode-aware `<figure data-viz="…">` blocks with custom interactive diagrams, syntax-highlighted code (sugar-high, Tokyo Night token palette), footnotes, and inline video with poster frames and spoiler-gated reveals. The result is a shell that costs nothing to maintain and set-pieces where they earn their keep.
color_typography: Near-monochrome. Light mode: `--bg: #fff`, `--text-copy: #171717`, `--text-heading: #000`, `--text-nav: #6b7280`, borders #e5e5e5 — plus a full shadcn/ui token set (Tailwind v4, tokens emitted in both hex and `lab()`). Dark mode inverts to zinc-950/zinc-200 territory. Accent colour is used almost nowhere in the chrome; the only saturated palette in the CSS belongs to the code-highlighting tokens (`--sh-class: #7aa2f7`, `--sh-string: #9ece6a`, `--sh-keyword: #bb9af7`, etc. — Tokyo Night) and to chart colours inside the essay visualisations. Typography: **STIX Two Text** (serif, loaded as a next/font CSS module applied on `<html>`) for document text — a deliberate publishing-not-product signal; Geist Sans and Geist Mono are available as CSS variables for UI and code; the visualisation figures explicitly opt back into sans (`font-sans`). Links are styled as underlines with a lightened decoration colour and a hover transition rather than a colour change. Dark mode is implemented with `next-themes` (`attribute="class"`, `defaultTheme="system"`, `enableSystem`, `disableTransitionOnChange`) and an inline pre-hydration script that reads localStorage then falls back to `prefers-color-scheme` — but there is **no visible theme toggle anywhere on the site**, so in practice dark mode simply follows the OS. Weaker than satnaing.dev on this one axis.
motion: Minimal in the chrome, meaningful in the content. The shell has essentially two animations: `transition-colors` on link underline-decoration hover, and `disableTransitionOnChange` on the theme provider specifically to suppress a flash. There are no scroll reveals, no parallax, no page transitions, no custom cursor, no loader. Inside essays, framer-motion powers the interactive visualisations (the template repo lists framer-motion ^12) — animated token streams, attention weights, a temperature slider, a training-loop stepper — and these are user-initiated controls (`aria-pressed`, `aria-checked` on the toggles) rather than autoplaying decoration. `prefers-reduced-motion` appears **zero times** in the shipped CSS, so the essay visualisations are not motion-gated; the practical harm is limited because almost all of that motion is triggered by an explicit click rather than by scroll or on-load, and the chrome itself has nothing to reduce. Inline video in /bio is behind explicit spoiler/reveal disclosures rather than autoplaying.
responsiveness_mobile: Excellent, and this is the structural payoff of the writing-led format_genre: a single centred prose column has essentially nothing to degrade. There are only two breakpoints in the entire stylesheet's layout logic (min-width 360px and 1400px, plus Tailwind's md/lg/xl for a handful of utilities), because the layout is one column at every size — the only responsive change on the homepage is `mt-0 md:mt-16` (drop the top margin on phones). No hamburger menu is needed because there is no nav to collapse. The measure is set in `ch`, so it reflows naturally. Where mobile care is actually visible is in the essay set-pieces: each `<figure data-viz>` is width-capped (`max-w-[680px]`), `w-full`, `overflow-hidden`, and the global stylesheet forces `table { display: block; overflow-x: auto; white-space: nowrap }` so wide tables scroll inside themselves rather than breaking the page — the correct pattern. Costs: the seven interactive visualisations in /ai are dense diagrams on a ~360px viewport and depend on tap targets sized for a cursor [uncertain how well they hold up on a small phone]; /ai is a ~180 KB HTML document, so a single essay is a heavier download than most portfolios' entire homepage; and with no nav at all, a mobile reader who lands mid-corpus has exactly one way back — the small grey byline link.
framework_hosting: Next.js 16 App Router with React 19, built with Turbopack, deployed on Vercel (headers: `server: Vercel`, `x-vercel-cache: HIT`, `x-nextjs-prerender: 1`, `x-nextjs-stale-time: 300`, `x-vercel-id: fra1::iad1::…`), fully prerendered with ISR and served from the edge. Styling is Tailwind CSS v4 (tokens compiled to `lab()` colour space, `@property` registrations, shadcn/ui token set). Content is MDX via @next/mdx with a custom `mdx-components.tsx` mapping; code highlighting is sugar-high; animation is framer-motion; there is a Postgres-backed redirects table (the `postgres` dependency plus a `redirects` table schema documented in the template README) which explains the 308s on /resume and /uses. Fonts: STIX Two Text plus Geist Sans/Mono, self-hosted through next/font. Domain is his own name on .com — the strongest possible personal-brand TLD signal, and short enough to say out loud in a talk. Deployment IDs are stamped on every asset URL (`?dpl=dpl_…`). Note that the site is on the current release of the framework its author spent five years evangelising — the dogfooding is the point.
performance_a11y: Performance: very good, with one caveat. The homepage is 21.7 KB of HTML (all content in the markup, prerendered, cache HIT, ~0.15 s TTFB from the edge), one 84 KB uncompressed stylesheet, and roughly 447 KB uncompressed JS across nine chunks — with no images, no web-font blocking, and no third-party scripts beyond Vercel Analytics. That is a lean homepage by any standard and dramatically leaner than satnaing.dev (80 KB HTML + ~680 KB JS) for a comparable render. The caveat is per-essay weight: /ai is ~180 KB of HTML on its own because the seven visualisations are server-rendered inline, so the flagship content page is roughly 8× the homepage. Accessibility: solid on fundamentals, thin on affordances. Good — `lang="en"` set, exactly one `<h1>` per page with `id` anchors on every heading, semantic `<main>`/`<ul>`/`<figure>`, real text everywhere (nothing is image-only), high monochrome contrast in both themes, `focus-visible` handling present in the CSS, an `sr-only` utility in use, external links carry `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, the interactive visualisations expose `aria-label` (27), `aria-pressed` (10) and `aria-checked` (18) on their controls and mark purely decorative parts `aria-hidden` (19), and `<figure>` elements are correctly `not-prose`-scoped. Missing — **no skip link** (mitigated, though not excused, by the fact that there is no nav to skip past: the first focusable element is already inside the content), **no `prefers-reduced-motion` handling at all**, no visible dark-mode toggle for users whose OS setting doesn't match their need, and no `<noscript>` fallback for the interactive figures. SEO/discoverability oddities: **robots.txt returns 404**, and while sitemap.xml exists with 74 URLs it is partly broken — it lists `https://leerob.com/.` (trailing dot) and 45 `/_glossary/<term>` URLs that all return 404 when fetched directly, so more than half the declared sitemap is dead. There is also **no RSS or Atom feed** (/rss, /rss.xml, /feed, /feed.xml, /llms.txt all 404), which for a writing-led site is a genuine gap — the newsletter and X are the only subscribe paths, and neither is linked from the homepage.
analytics_instrumentation: Vercel Analytics only — the `@vercel/analytics` client is bundled (a small 6.6 KB chunk containing the `va.vercel-scripts` beacon and the Analytics component) alongside Next.js's built-in Web Vitals reporting. Nothing else: no Google Analytics, no Plausible, Umami, Fathom, PostHog, Hotjar or session replay, no tag manager, no ad pixels. No cookie or consent banner — consistent with Vercel Analytics being cookieless. First-party only, which is the cleanest instrumentation profile of any site in this set.
project_presentation:
There are no project cards, no gallery, no demos, and no repo grid — the deliberate absence is the finding. Nothing on this site is presented in the 'screenshot + description + tech tags + Live Demo / GitHub' format that defines every other portfolio in this research set, and there is no page that lists what he has built. Work is surfaced in four indirect ways instead:

1. **Employment as narrative essay.** /cursor and /vercel are dated experience pages written as prose. /cursor ('July 2025 – Present') describes creating and maintaining Cursor's docs and learning courses, speaking on context engineering and the Composer model, and playing pseudo-PM on launches, then the June 2026 move to ML — with in-prose links to the actual docs and courses as evidence, plus an embedded video. /vercel is a retrospective ('5 Things I Learned From 5 Years At Vercel') carrying the growth numbers and behind-the-scenes photos.

2. **Projects as essay subjects.** The one build that gets real treatment is Pixo, and it appears as an essay — 'Building Low-Level Software with Only Coding Agents' (/pixo) — described on /stack as 'my latest experiment using only coding agents, if you want an in-depth example'. The write-up IS the presentation; there is no card and no demo button.

3. **The essays themselves as the portfolio.** /ai is the flagship artifact: a long-form explainer shipping seven bespoke interactive visualisations (next-token prediction, tokenization, embeddings, self-attention, temperature, training loop, RLHF) built with framer-motion, 14 footnotes, and — notably — external references routed through web.archive.org snapshots to survive link rot. The demonstration of engineering and design ability is the artifact you are reading, not a link to something elsewhere.

4. **A single 'code' link.** The word 'code' in the homepage's closing paragraph links to github.com/leerob (39 public repos, ~16k followers). That is the entirety of the repo surface.

Live-demo availability is therefore N/A by design — there is nothing framed as a demo. The nearest equivalents are /music (a live Spotify integration showing top artists and tracks) and /bookmarks (a large curated link library), and note that **/music is currently broken**: both panels read 'No data available.', a visible dead integration on a live page.
resume_integration_mode: None of the four modes, and unusually, this is a documented removal rather than an omission: **/resume returns a 308 permanent redirect to `/`**, as does /uses. There is no PDF, no inline HTML CV, and nothing an ATS could parse into structured employment records — a resume parser fed this URL would extract a name, a two-clause self-description, and prose. The substitutes are /bio (narrative life story), /cursor and /vercel (dated narrative role pages), and LinkedIn (linked only from the JSON-LD `sameAs` array, not from any visible page). He also points readers at third-party biographical sources instead of maintaining his own: /bio closes with 'If you want my AI-generated bio, you can read more on Grokipedia' and 'I was also profiled in Arena Magazine in March 2026'. This is what the senior-career endpoint looks like — the resume is delegated outward because inbound no longer arrives through application funnels.
proof_verifiability: High, but through mechanisms a junior engineer cannot copy. The strongest proof is that the artifact is the evidence: the /ai essay with its seven hand-built interactive visualisations demonstrates frontend and explanatory ability directly, and the site itself demonstrates that he ships on the framework he spent five years evangelising. Verifiable specifics: the Vercel growth numbers (30 people/$1M ARR in 2020 → 650 people/$200M+ ARR in 2025) are public-record figures rather than self-reported personal metrics; the Cursor role page links out to the actual docs and courses he built, and names the colleagues he worked with (Eric, Roman, Ben) — attributable and checkable; the JSON-LD Person block declares `alumniOf` Iowa State University and `sameAs` for X, GitHub, YouTube and LinkedIn, so identity is machine-cross-referenceable; external validation is pointed at rather than claimed (Grokipedia, an Arena Magazine profile in March 2026); and a genuinely admirable craft detail — outbound references in /ai are wrapped in **web.archive.org snapshots**, so the citations survive link rot, which is a stronger citation practice than most technical blogs and nearly all portfolios. Weaknesses: the advising and angel-investing claims have zero supporting detail — no portfolio list, no company names, no track record, purely 'trust me'; there are no dates on most essays beyond a month/year byline; the JSON-LD `jobTitle` ('VP of Developer Experience') contradicts the body copy ('I work on ML at Cursor'), a small factual inconsistency in the machine-readable layer; and the site's core proposition — 15 years coding, teaching millions — rests on off-site reputation that the site never bothers to substantiate because it assumes you already know.
quantified_impact: Present, but exclusively as narrative company metrics rather than as portfolio-style personal metrics — and never in a stat block. The concrete numbers are: Vercel from 30 people and ~$1M ARR (2020) to 650 people and $200M+ ARR (2025), with a personal trajectory of 'IC to VP'; Cursor joined at ~70 employees with 'a tiny marketing team'; 15 years coding and 'teaching for the second half'; 'helping teach millions of developers to build on the web' (/bio); two React/Next.js courses created before joining Vercel; a move to ML in June 2026. Off-site scale that the site never mentions: ~16k GitHub followers, and the template descended from his site repo sitting at ~7.6k stars and ~1.45k forks. What is entirely absent: any latency/accuracy/uptime/conversion/cost-saved figure, any per-project metric, any dashboard or stat tiles, any 'X% improvement' claim. The pattern is worth naming for the report — every number on this site is embedded in a sentence inside a story, and the credibility comes from the surrounding narrative rather than from the digit. Also note a quantification feature that is currently failing: /music is a live Spotify top-artists/top-tracks integration and both sections render 'No data available.'
content_freshness:
Very fresh, and freshness is demonstrated by publication rather than asserted. The newest essay, 'How we teach AI models' (/model-behavior), is dated **July 2026 — the current month**. /cursor is maintained as a living page ('July 2025 – Present') and was updated to reflect the June 2026 move to the ML team; /ai carries an explicit revision byline, 'November 2024 (updated 2026)', which is the correct way to keep an evergreen explainer honest. The homepage's opening paragraph is current to the ML role. The descendant template repo saw dependency bumps on 2026-07-28 (two days before research), and the deployed build carries a live Vercel deployment ID. There is no 'currently working on' widget, no now-page, no last-updated footer and no changelog — the recency signal is entirely 'the top item on /writing is from this month'.

Three staleness tells against that: **/music is broken** ('No data available.' for both top artists and top tracks — a dead Spotify integration sitting on a live page); the **JSON-LD still says `jobTitle: "VP of Developer Experience"`** while the visible copy says he works on ML at Cursor; and the **sitemap declares 45 `/_glossary/<term>` URLs plus a malformed `https://leerob.com/.` entry, all of which 404** — the sitemap has drifted from the routes. Combined with the missing robots.txt and the absent RSS feed, the machine-facing surface is measurably less well maintained than the human-facing one.
writing_tone: Plain, declarative, confident, and almost entirely adjective-free — the tonal opposite of the standard portfolio register. Sentences are short and lead with the fact: 'I'm an engineer and writer. I work on ML at Cursor, helping improve model behavior.' No 'passionate', no 'exceptional results', no 'unique combination of skills'; the only grand statement is a genuine mission line — 'My life's work is to make technology easy to understand and interesting to learn about' — immediately grounded by 'I'm a husband, father, and a massive music fan.' Long-form voice is teacherly and analogy-driven: /model-behavior explains model training via a helpful colleague and a basketball player ('Knowledge and experience are two different stats… book smarts versus street smarts'); /ai frames itself with unusual humility ('Not to become an expert, but to gain an appreciation for the abstractions I use every day… written for other engineers who are new to topics like…'). /bio is warm, specific and self-deprecating, including admitting to pirating creative software as a kid ('found ways to (ahem) completely legally download it'). /vercel is candid about failure modes ('passion without boundaries will lead you to burnout', 'Why was I responding to tweets on the beach? I hadn't built the system for others to take ownership') and closes on 'I'm damn proud to be an engineer.' The register is 'competent adult explaining something they understand', and the absence of self-marketing language is itself the strongest status signal on the page.
standout_features:
Ranked by borrowability, since almost none of this site's *architecture* transfers down-market but several of its *techniques* do.

CHEAP AND WORTH STEALING AT ANY SENIORITY:
1. **One-word top-level URLs for every page** (/ai, /agents, /css, /stack, /bio, /beliefs, /compression, /rust, /heroku). Memorable, quotable on a slide, typeable from memory, and free. Back them with a redirects table so nothing ever 404s. The single most copyable idea here.
2. **The byline IS the home link.** The grey attribution line under each title ('By Lee Robinson', 'November 2024 (updated 2026) – Lee Robinson') is an `<a href="/">`. This is how the site gets away with having no nav at all — one element doing two jobs, zero pixels of chrome.
3. **Revision-aware datelines** — 'November 2024 (updated 2026)' — instead of a single publish date. Costs one string and converts an ageing evergreen post from a liability into a maintained asset. Directly addresses the failure mode visible on satnaing.dev.
4. **Outbound citations wrapped in web.archive.org snapshots**, so references survive link rot. Rare craft; costs one paste per link.
5. **Employment history written as dated narrative pages** (/cursor 'July 2025 – Present', /vercel) rather than a bullet timeline, with in-prose links to the actual artifacts produced and the colleagues involved. More persuasive per word than any Experience list, and it doubles as content.
6. **/bio as 'My life in five minutes'** — an origin story with embedded video and spoiler-gated reveals. Almost no engineer writes one, it is the page people actually remember, and it costs an afternoon.
7. **Serif document font (STIX Two Text) at a ~60ch measure, monochrome, no accent colour.** Signals 'publication' rather than 'product landing page' for the price of one font declaration, and makes long-form actually pleasant to read.
8. **Deleting rather than keeping** — /resume and /uses 308 to the homepage. The willingness to remove pages that no longer serve the argument is what keeps the site legible.
9. **A prose CTA as the last sentence rather than a button** — 'I also make videos, advise companies, and do angel investing. Reach out if interested.' One mailto, no form.
10. **First-party, cookieless analytics only** (Vercel Analytics), no consent banner needed.

MEDIUM-TO-HIGH COST BUT DEFENSIBLE:
11. **Interactive visualisations as the proof-of-skill artifact.** Seven bespoke framer-motion diagrams inside /ai — tokenization, embeddings, self-attention, next-token prediction, temperature, training loop, RLHF — each in a bordered, dark-mode-aware, width-capped `<figure>`. This is the substitute for a project gallery: instead of linking to demos, the essay *is* the demo. A mid-level engineer could ship one such figure inside one write-up and get most of the differentiating effect.
12. **A 45-term AI glossary corpus** (attention, tokenization, RLHF, KV cache, speculative decoding, scaling laws, reward hacking, mixture-of-experts…) supporting the essays — an educational moat that makes the site a reference rather than a read-once page. Caveat: it is currently mis-plumbed (see below).
13. **/bookmarks as a large curated link library** organised into Tools / Articles / Productivity / Craft / Engineering. Cheap to maintain, high return-visit value, and a taste signal.
14. **/beliefs and /stack as opinionated essays** standing in for a values page and a skills list. Both convert a boring section into shareable content.

ANTI-PATTERNS THIS SITE DEMONSTRATES (do not copy):
15. **No RSS/Atom feed on a writing-led site** (/rss, /rss.xml, /feed, /feed.xml all 404) and **no robots.txt**. For a site whose entire strategy is publishing, this is a self-inflicted distribution wound.
16. **A broken sitemap** — 45 `/_glossary/*` URLs and a malformed `https://leerob.com/.` entry, all 404 — i.e. more than half the declared sitemap is dead, and the glossary corpus is unreachable to crawlers and readers alike.
17. **A visibly dead integration on a live page** — /music renders 'No data available.' for both Spotify panels. If a live-data page can break, it will; either monitor it or make it static.
18. **Stale structured data** — JSON-LD `jobTitle: "VP of Developer Experience"` contradicting the body copy.
19. **No `prefers-reduced-motion` handling and no visible dark-mode toggle**, despite shipping animated figures and a class-based theme provider.

THE STRUCTURAL LESSON FOR THE REPORT: this site works because the author's reputation arrives before the visitor does. Strip the name and you strip the site's function — there is no gallery, no resume, no metric block, nothing to evaluate a stranger by. It is therefore the correct *aspiration* and the wrong *starting point*: borrow the URL scheme, the byline-as-nav trick, the revision datelines, the narrative career pages and the one-strong-interactive-essay play; do not borrow the removal of the projects section.
originality_vs_template: Custom build with an unusual twist: the template lineage runs *outward* from this site, not into it. The repository that once held the personal-site source (leerob/site, and before that leerob/leerob.io) has been renamed and genericised into **leerob/next-mdx-blog** — a 'Next.js + MDX blog template' with placeholder 'John Smith' metadata, ~7.6k stars and ~1.45k forks — so the site became a template that thousands of other developers now fork, while the live site itself evolved well beyond it (the current leerob.com has the glossary corpus, the interactive visualisations and the STIX Two Text typography, none of which are in the template). Its influence is directly attested inside this research set: satnaing.dev's own README lists 'Lee Robinson Website' as its first design credit. There are no starter-kit fingerprints in the live build — the shell is hand-written App Router + MDX, and the essay visualisations are bespoke. Design lineage, if any, is the serif-minimal personal-blog convention (Bear Blog / plaintext / Gwern-adjacent), arrived at independently rather than forked.
source_available: Partially, and it has drifted. The current live site's exact source does **not** appear to be public: the repo that historically held it (leerob/site → previously leerob/leerob.io) now 301-redirects to **github.com/leerob/next-mdx-blog**, which has been stripped down to a generic template — placeholder 'John Smith' metadata, `metadataBase: next-mdx-blog.vercel.app`, an Inter font instead of STIX Two Text, three dummy `app/n/1|2|3` notes, and a `"delete": "rm -rf app/n"` script — with none of leerob.com's glossary, visualisations or essays [uncertain whether a separate private repo or a differently-named public repo now holds the live source]. What IS public and useful: that template (~7.6k stars, ~1.45k forks, no LICENSE file, last pushed 2026-07-28, Next.js 16.2 / React 19.1 / Tailwind 4 / @next/mdx / framer-motion / sugar-high / postgres / @vercel/analytics, Turbopack for dev and build) documents the exact stack the live site is built on, including the Postgres `redirects` table that explains the /resume and /uses 308s. So the dogfooding signal is strong but indirect: he open-sourced the *pattern* and kept the *instance* private — the inverse of satnaing.dev, which published the instance itself. The homepage's single 'code' link points to his GitHub profile (39 public repos, ~16k followers) rather than to the site repo.
contact_methods: One channel, one sentence, no chrome. The entire contact surface is the last sentence of the homepage: 'I also make videos, advise companies, and do angel investing. Reach out if interested.' — where 'Reach out' is `mailto:lee@leerob.com`. No contact form, no Calendly, no newsletter signup, no phone, no availability status, and — remarkably — **no social-links row anywhere on the site**, because there is no footer. Social presence is instead woven into the same closing paragraph as in-prose links: 'code' → github.com/leerob, 'follow me online' → x.com/leerob, 'videos' → youtube.com/@leerob. LinkedIn (linkedin.com/in/leeerob) appears **only** in the JSON-LD `sameAs` array — machine-readable but not clickable by a human, which is a deliberate signal about which channels he wants used. His Substack newsletter (leerob.substack.com) is not linked from the homepage at all. Placement consequence: contact is reachable only from the bottom of the homepage; a reader who lands on an essay has no contact affordance except the byline link back to /.
pii_exposure: Minimal and well-judged. The only contact detail is a first-name address on his own domain (lee@leerob.com) — no personal Gmail, no phone number, no postal address, no calendar link. Real name and general location (Des Moines, Iowa) are public by intent since the name is the brand and the domain. The notable exposure is voluntary and biographical rather than technical: /bio discusses his marriage (2020), becoming a father (2024), his daughters, his parents' 40-year construction business, his hometown ('my public school class had 32 students', 'no stoplights'), and includes an admission of pirating creative software as a teenager — all deliberate narrative choices by someone whose brand is candour, not leakage. Family members are referenced but not named, and no photographs of children are surfaced in the served HTML [uncertain, since /bio embeds video clips whose contents were not inspected]. No avatar or personal photo appears on the homepage; avatar.png exists but is referenced only from JSON-LD. Visitor-side privacy is the cleanest in this research set: first-party cookieless Vercel Analytics only, no third-party scripts, no tag manager, no ad pixels, no consent banner required, and no client-side calls to third-party APIs that would disclose visitor IPs.
